India exported about $863 billion in FY26. The target is $2 trillion by 2030-31!!!

The Hindu BusinessLine reports that Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal wants exporters, especially MSMEs, to be far more aggressive in FTA partner markets: bigger trade fairs, more buyer-seller meets and more use of the Export Promotion Mission. India has concluded or operationalised FTAs with eight partners, including the UAE, Australia, the UK and the EU, which is yet to be implemented.

Mint asks the harder question. Bank of America estimates that only 20–30% of India's eligible exports use FTA preferences, against 60–70% in developed markets. Sanjay Notani of Economic Laws Practice puts it well: businesses with finance, reliable suppliers and strong compliance systems move first.

I read that as a banking problem as much as a trade problem. Marketing gets you a buyer. Finance decides whether a small firm can fulfil the order.

The EPM, with an outlay of ₹25,060 crore over six years, has a credit arm, Niryat Protsahan, which the coverage mentions only briefly. The detail matters:

IIBF says MSME exporters get 2.75% a year interest subvention on rupee export credit, pre- and post-shipment, capped at ₹50 lakh per IEC for FY 2025-26.

IIBF also says collateral support runs with CGTMSE: up to 85% guarantee for micro and small exporters, 65% for medium, up to ₹10 crore per exporter a year.

For a small exporter, packing credit without heavy collateral is often the difference between bidding for a European order and letting it go. These tools exist. My worry is that many MSMEs and branch managers still treat them as paperwork rather than working capital.

The payments side is moving too. Recently, RBI set 9 months to realise and repatriate export proceeds, and cut the period for INR-invoiced exports from 18 to 12 months. Import payment timelines are now set by contract, with AD banks given more discretion. Business Standard reports the RBI also let AD banks lend in rupees to residents of Bhutan, Nepal and Sri Lanka to support cross-border trade.

Tighter realisation timelines mean exporters must price credit terms carefully, and banks must watch receivables in FTA markets more closely. Rupee settlement helps, but only where both sides are ready for it.

My view: FTA utilisation will rise when market access, compliance and trade finance move together. A trade fair stall is wasted if the exporter cannot fund the order or collect the payment on time.

#ExportFinance #FTA #MSME

What does it take for a bank founded over 200 years ago to remain relevant in a world where finance is changing every day? 🤔

That was one of the questions that made our group research on Citibank more interesting than just studying another financial institution. The story goes back to 1812, when Citi Bank of New York was established to help New York compete with other major financial centres. What started as a local banking institution gradually expanded its reach across countries and markets, eventually becoming part of the global financial powerhouse we know today as Citi.

As part of our group project at International School of Business and Media ISBM, we explored Citibank’s history, business model, market positioning and competitive landscape, comparing its strategies with major players like JPMorgan Chase, HSBC, Bank of America and Wells Fargo. But the most interesting takeaway for me was this, being a legacy brand doesn’t guarantee future success. The ability to adapt does.

From the evolution of ATMs and digital banking to the growing importance of wealth management, cross-border transactions and personalised financial services, the banking industry shows how innovation can reshape even the most established businesses.
We also explored how Citibank differentiates itself through its global network and institutional banking capabilities, while its competitors leverage their own strengths in retail banking, domestic markets and integrated financial services.
This project helped me look beyond numbers and financial products to understand the bigger picture, how history, customer expectations, competitive positioning and strategic decisions shape a brand’s future.

A valuable learning experience that connected business strategy with the real world and reminded me that understanding a company’s past can offer powerful insights into where it is heading next.
#Citibank #BusinessStrategy #MarketResearch #CompetitiveAnalysis #Banking #ISBMPune #PGDM

Is the Boom in Artificial Intelligence Spending a Bubble?

The use of artificial intelligence has generated one of the biggest buying frenzies in economic history.

According to Gartner, spending on artificial intelligence will reach $2.53 trillion in 2026 and rise to $3.33 trillion in 2027. Hyperscaler capital expenditure in the US economy is running at around 2% of GDP, and the growth of the country's GDP was driven largely by the investments in AI in early 2026.

Such big numbers inevitably lead to a question - Could we be facing another speculative bubble?

There certainly are valid concerns. In late June 2026, a sell-off of technology stocks occurred against the backdrop of doubts about the profitability of the massive spending in AI. 

Uncertain returns are the issue - Fewer than half of artificial intelligence projects generate profits for the companies, but executives still keep pouring money in their initiatives and there are lots of people trying to profit from the trend-
In Bank of America's October fund manager survey, 45% of participants pointed to owning global chip stocks as the most crowded trade. Some experts compare the current situation to the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when the enthusiasm had been far greater than the actual profitability of companies.

But there are important distinctions. 
Today's leading spenders on AI, such as Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon, are some of the most profitable companies ever.

According to some analysts, even if valuations fall, the data centers and networks that the corporations are building now, just as similar assets during previous booms, might preserve their value in the long run. Like the railway networks and fiber-optical cables of previous bubbles, they will survive even after the bust of speculative mania that preceded their creation.

So what extent can the current market conditions be considered a bubble, and how might the potential collapse of some companies and falling stock prices affect the long-term future of the technology? 

In conclusion, the truth probably lies somewhere in between while certain aspects of the current state of the markets have all features of the bubbles, and some companies will go bankrupt and some stock prices will go down sharply, the technology is here to stay.
#Economics #US #ArtificalTechnology

INDIA BEATS THE US TO BECOME THE WORLD'S LARGEST ECONOMY!

Yes, this could be the headline one day. And looking at the direction America is heading, I wonder if that day could arrive sooner than expected.

The United States created some of the world's most powerful AI technologies.
The United States is investing billions in AI infrastructure and data centres.
And now, some of America's own leading AI scientists are warning about the dangers of developing increasingly powerful AI without adequate safeguards.

Some have even raised concerns about existential risks to humanity.
But are America's biggest corporations listening?

Throughout the year, we've watched tech giants announce layoffs, restructure teams and invest aggressively in AI.

Companies are investing billions in AI while reducing their dependence on human resources. And now look at what's happening across America.

In just a few days, major technical disruptions have been reported involving:

Microsoft – Outlook, Teams and Microsoft 365
JPMorgan Chase – Banking and payment processing
Bank of America – Online banking and transactions
Wells Fargo – Digital banking services
U.S. Bank – Account access
Zelle – Money transfers

Even America's aviation infrastructure has experienced serious technical disruptions.

These aren't small companies. These are institutions that millions of people trust with their money, businesses and everyday lives.

And here's what I find deeply concerning.
Companies are treating human resources as an expense that can be reduced.
Experienced employees are losing jobs.
Automation is becoming a priority.
But when critical technology fails, who fixes it?

AI can automate processes. But can AI replace the experience, judgement and accountability of an entire workforce?

We don't have evidence that these outages were caused by AI or layoffs. But they raise an important question about how much corporations should prioritize cost-cutting over technical resilience.

Think about the consequences of these disruptions.
Millions of users potentially affected.
Banking transactions interrupted.
Businesses losing productivity.
Customers losing confidence.
And serious operational and financial risks for the companies involved.

What is the point of saving millions in employee salaries if one major system failure can put your entire business at risk?

I'm an entrepreneur. I build technology products. I believe in AI.
But I strongly disagree with the mindset that replacing humans should be the ultimate goal of technological progress.

And this is where I see an opportunity for India.
America may be leading the AI race today.
But India has the talent, ambition and technological capabilities to build a powerful economy of its own.

Maybe the next global economic leader won't be the country that replaces the most employees with AI.

Maybe it will be the country that understands how to make AI and humans work together.

#India #USEconomy #ArtificialIntelligence #Layoffs #Microsoft

‣ Berkshire Hathaway holds $365 to 400 billion in cash — Apple built one of the largest corporate cash piles in history — these are not failures of capital allocation, they are the output of exceptional business models and disciplined deployment standards

‣ Cash is insurance against permanent capital impairment — a 10% increase in cash holdings is associated with meaningfully lower corporate distress risk — the businesses that entered 2008 and COVID with liquidity avoided the forced asset sales and dilutive financing that permanently impaired their less prepared peers

‣ Berkshire’s 2008 crisis interventions — capital provided to Goldman Sachs and Bank of America on extraordinarily favourable terms — were possible only because the cash was already there — strategic dry powder requires accumulation before the opportunity appears, not after

‣ Software, platform, and branded consumer businesses generate cash faster than reinvestment opportunities can absorb it at acceptable returns — the cash pile is the consequence of business model quality, not evidence of deployment failure

‣ Excess cash is genuinely suboptimal when governance is weak — managers who accumulate cash to preserve autonomy rather than because deployment opportunities fail the return threshold are consuming shareholder capital — the empirical evidence shows cash creates value with strong governance and destroys value without it

‣ The discipline of not deploying capital simply because it is available — of saying no to mediocre uses even when appearing inactive draws criticism — is the hallmark of genuine capital allocation excellence and is genuinely difficult to sustain

‣ Cash is oxygen — it keeps the business alive when everything goes wrong — but oxygen is not a meal, and the businesses that understand the difference are the ones that compound over decades

The October 2026 enforcement ledger: The top 5 cases!

1. TD Bank, N.A. (DOJ / FinCEN / OCC)
The Breach: Willful AML program failure driven by a cost-cutting culture that capped compliance resources. This created unmonitored payment channels, enabling over $1.5B in suspicious flows ($400M linked to narcotics) to bypass basic oversight.
The Quantum: $3.09 Billion global financial penalty and a historic OCC asset cap.
Strategic Priorities: Overhauling core data governance frameworks, validating backlogged SAR queues, and scaling transaction monitoring throughput under rigorous independent oversight.

2. Bank of America (FinCEN / OCC / OFAC)
The Breach: Failure to remediate a 2024 cease-and-desist, creating acute backlogs within its transaction monitoring system (TMS). Failed to file timely SARs on $5B+ in trade-based money laundering (TBML) flows, while outdated filters let $14M route through blocked accounts.
The Quantum: $1.21 Billion total financial penalty.
Strategic Priorities: Integrating automated change management to dynamically map audit findings into active detection rules, backed by end-to-end data lineage tracing.

3. American Express National Bank (OCC)
The Breach: Chronic BSA deficiencies over a ten-year horizon. Failed to execute adequate risk assessments, allowing $13B in high-risk transactions to bypass standard lookback thresholds.
The Quantum: $350 Million civil money penalty and a cease-and-desist order.
Strategic Priorities: Calibrating risk models to dynamically shift alert thresholds based on sudden variations in cross-border volume and counterparty country risk.

4. Federal Student Aid Title IV Fraud Network (FinCEN)
The Breach: Deficient digital identity verification and downstream monitoring, allowing fraud syndicates to exploit onboarding gaps and launder $270M in federal disbursements.
The Quantum: $270 Million in disrupted illicit flows referred to law enforcement.
Strategic Priorities: Deploying risk-proportionate digital onboarding controls—such as device fingerprinting and velocity checking—to isolate high-velocity, multi-account routing networks.

5. Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (SEB) Baltic Branch (NYDFS)
The Breach: Severe transaction monitoring failures within Baltic subsidiary networks that contaminated the NY clearing system, caused by compliance understaffing and multi-year alert backlogs.
The Quantum: $33 Million regulatory fine.
Strategic Priorities: Establishing continuous model validation protocols that align analyst capacity with alert volume, eliminating silos between foreign subsidiaries.

Transitioning from check-the-box exercises to live data integrity and model optimization is no longer a strategic recommendation; it is a baseline prerequisite for compliance survival.

#AI | #Banking : AI Agents are Forcing Banks to Rewrite Terms and Conditions for Online Access of Banking Accounts. Major U.S. banks have recently tightened their rules to block third-party AI agents from logging into customer accounts or making transactions directly. This is specifically about AI agents, not a blanket ban on every human agent, power of attorney, or authorized representative.

What banks are doing :

1. Citi says it does not permit third-party AI agents or assistants to log into customer accounts or transact directly through its digital banking platforms; limited read-only access may be available through approved open-banking providers.

2. JPMorgan Chase is blocking outside AI agents from using customer credentials to access account information or move money, while allowing limited view-only data retrieval through intermediaries such as Plaid.

3. Bank of America is restricting AI-agent access to consumer deposit accounts while it develops rules for liability when an AI tool authorizes a payment.

4. Wells Fargo has updated its online access agreement, effective November 24, to address third-party AI agents: customers are responsible for supervising agents, and transactions by authorized representatives—including agents—may be treated as authorized unless the customer notifies the bank and the bank has a reasonable opportunity to act.

Are Indian Banks Geared Up for Agentic Banking?

FinTech Unwrapped

Banks are reporting real gains from AI coding. Cutting engineering teams too quickly could limit what those gains are worth.

Bank of America reports a 20%+ improvement in general coding, with around 19,000 internal users. BNP Paribas puts developer productivity gains at 15%. Barclays reports a 15% improvement across the software development lifecycle.

At that scale, AI is freeing up meaningful capacity.

Having worked in product, I know how much valuable work sits in a bank’s backlog because engineering teams cannot get to it. An unreliable payment flow can remain unresolved while the team handles urgent maintenance.

AI gives banks room to tackle more of that work.

Yet some are already turning productivity gains into lower headcount. Barclays’ planned 5,000 job cuts include developer roles, with AI cited alongside wider technology improvements.

There is a trade-off here. Removing capacity as soon as it becomes available may leave a bank delivering roughly the same service at a lower cost.

I would give teams time to show what they can achieve with it first. Fixing problems that drive customers away could be worth more than the salaries saved.

Biriyani or Bot
My phone has two pairs of lookalikes. Swiggy and Claude are both orange. Blinkit and Rapido are both yellow. My thumb knows the colour but not the name, so some mornings I am typing onions  when Rapido asks where to and some evenings I am looking at delectable chats when I meant to open a spreadsheet.
On a phone, that is harmless. Inside company systems, the same mix-up is happening with much more at stake.
Banks are now spotting AI agents that log in to customer accounts and act there. Reuters reported that they are detecting and deleting unauthorized third-party agents, and that JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America and Schwab all say agents cannot move customer money, though read-only functions such as viewing balances are allowed.
The concern seems to be that an agent logged in with a customer's credentials looks exactly like the customer. The bank sees the same login, so it cannot tell which one is acting.
Now look at your own company. An AP agent is set up with the finance manager's ERP login, because that was the quickest way. On a Sunday at 2:14 a.m., a journal entry is posted. The audit log says the manager posted it. The manager was asleep.
Nothing was hacked. The log is accurate about the login and wrong about the actor. Maker and checker, segregation of duties and every review of who did what assume the log names a person, and with a borrowed login it cannot.
What the banks are enforcing is what finance should ask of its own agents:
* Its own identity. A separate account for each agent, never a person's login.
* Read-only by default. Write access is granted one action at a time.
* Access that expires, so a permission given for one task does not last for a year.
* A log that records both parties: "agent X, acting for Y".
It takes a small rigour to set up. A log that cannot tell the person from the agent is not an audit trail and is dangerous
